title: India's First Private Orbital Rocket Vikram-1 Set for Historic Launch From Sriharikota
excerpt: Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 is India's first private orbital rocket, launching on July 18.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 is India's first private orbital rocket, launching on July 18.
  • The rocket can carry payloads up to 350 kg to Low Earth Orbit with advanced technologies.
  • Skyroot achieved unicorn status after raising $60 million, now valued at $1 billion.
  • A successful launch could position India as a competitor in the global small satellite market.

  • Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 is scheduled to launch on July 18 at 11:30 AM IST from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, making it India's first private orbital rocket attempt.
  • The seven-storey-tall rocket, built with an all-carbon composite structure and 3D-printed engines, can carry payloads up to 350 kg to Low Earth Orbit.
  • The Hyderabad-based startup, valued at $1 billion after raising $60 million from GIC and Sherpalo Ventures, is carrying domestic and international payloads on Mission Aagaman.
  • A successful flight would position India's private space sector as a credible competitor in the global small satellite launch market.

Skyroot Aerospace is poised to make Indian space history with the launch of Vikram-1, the country's first privately developed orbital-class rocket. The mission, christened Aagaman — meaning "arrival" — is scheduled for liftoff at 11:30 AM IST on July 18 from the first launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh.

If successful, Skyroot will become the first Indian company after ISRO to send a rocket into orbit from Indian soil, marking a pivotal moment for the country's rapidly expanding private space ecosystem.

What Is Vikram-1?

![Satish Dhawan Space Centre — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/90/LVM3_M3%2C_OneWeb_India-2_campaign_30.webp)

Standing roughly 20 metres tall and measuring 1.7 metres in diameter, Vikram-1 is a four-stage orbital launch vehicle designed to carry small satellites weighing up to 350 kg into Low Earth Orbit. The first three stages use solid rocket motors, while the fourth employs a liquid engine for precise orbital insertion.

The rocket features several advanced technologies: an all-carbon composite structure that reduces weight, 3D-printed engines, and high-performance solid-fuel boosters. These design choices aim to make launches both cost-effective and reliable — critical factors in the competitive small satellite launch market.

> **"The rocket also carries Cosmos Diamonds' artwork "Cosmic Bloom," a diamond-studded art piece, and a micro-art creation."**

"We have done everything that could be done to test Vikram-1 on ground. On 18 July, we are eager to see how Vikram-1 performs in a real flight environment for the first time."

— Pawan Kumar Chandana, Co-founder and CEO, Skyroot Aerospace

The Mission Details

![Low Earth Orbit — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/20/ISS-44_Milky_Way.jpg)

Mission Aagaman will carry technology demonstration payloads from Grahaa Space, Cosmoserve, and Germany's DCubed, along with Skyroot's own SCOPE payload. The rocket also carries Cosmos Diamonds' artwork "Cosmic Bloom," a diamond-studded art piece, and a micro-art creation. In a ceremonial touch, Vikram-1 will carry handwritten notes from Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Indian-origin astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla.

The mission targets an orbit at an altitude of 450 km with a 60-degree orbital inclination. While this is primarily a test flight — designed to collect in-flight performance data across propulsion, guidance, and stage separation systems — it already carries paying customers, a signal of commercial confidence in Skyroot's capabilities.

From Vikram-S to Vikram-1

Mission Aagaman: Key Details
›Launch Date: July 18, 2023
›Launch Site: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota
›Orbit Target: 450 km altitude
›Payloads: Domestic and international customers

This launch marks Skyroot's second mission overall, following the successful suborbital flight of Vikram-S on November 18, 2022. That earlier mission demonstrated the company's ability to reach space but did not attempt orbit. Vikram-1 represents a far more ambitious step — and the one that could transform Skyroot from a promising startup into a functioning launch provider.

![Andhra Pradesh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Tirumala_090615.jpg/3840px-Tirumala_090615.jpg)

Founded by former ISRO engineers, the Hyderabad-based company achieved unicorn status after raising $60 million from GIC and Sherpalo Ventures in May. It has since developed both Vikram-1 and the larger Vikram-2, which is designed to carry 900 kg payloads.

Why It Matters for India's Space Economy

The launch comes as India opens its state-dominated space sector to private companies, seeking a bigger share of the global satellite launch market. Industrial groups such as Larsen & Toubro and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited are also moving into rocket manufacturing as the government pushes to build a $44 billion space economy by 2033, according to Reuters.

The small satellite launch market is deeply supply-constrained. Companies like Rocket Lab and Firefly Aerospace have established positions, but demand for LEO satellite services — communications, Earth observation, weather forecasting — continues to outstrip available launch capacity. A successful Vikram-1 mission would add a credible Indian alternative to that roster.

What to Watch

ISRO has opened viewing gallery registrations for the launch at its Sriharikota facility. This is the second launch from the spaceport in 2026, following the PSLV C62 mission in January that failed due to a stage-III anomaly — a reminder that rocketry remains an inherently uncertain business. For Skyroot and India's private space sector, the next few hours will determine whether years of development translate into orbit.
